11926-washington-in-domestic-life-from-o:
Richard Rush's Washington in Domestic Life, published in 1857, draws on original letters and manuscripts to present Washington at home. Rush, in confiding the brief paper to his publishers, offers to bear any deficiency in the cost of publishing after their charges are defrayed. That is a modest preface to a modest book.

The study concentrates on character as shown in household matters: correspondence, manners, and the management of Mount Vernon, rather than on campaigns or presidencies. For readers who knew Washington mainly as general and president, Rush's domestic portrait supplied a different scale. It shows how a public man's private habits and letters reveal the temper behind his public decisions.
13517-in-bohemia-with-du-maurier-the-fir:
Felix Moscheles remembers Bohemian days with George du Maurier in this first series of reminiscences, with sixty-three original drawings by du Maurier of the artist's life in the fifties. Moscheles wrote his introduction and posted last proofs shortly before du Maurier's death reached him in Venice, turning sunshine to darkness.

Du Maurier could draw and Moscheles paint, du Maurier sing and Moscheles mesmerise, and both talk beautifully, making them bright stars in Carry's firmament. A drawing shows a double-bedded room in Brussels at eleven, with Bobtail washing a smutty face and Rag putting on tight boots while smoking three pipes. Moscheles writes affectionate, art-filled memories of youth.
19273-the-dead-men-s-song-being-the-stor:
Champion Ingraham Hitchcock wrote this 1914 Louisville volume on Young Ewing Allison and his poem The Dead Men's Song. Only two hundred and fifty copies were made, with facsimiles of manuscripts and a photograph of Allison. Walt Mason's line opens the book: a poet of such a song deserves knell and praise.

Hitchcock recalls Allison's office habits, his desk-cleaning parties spring and fall, dust, torn papers, and humming of Bing-Binger the Baritone Singer. Letters were boxed to a warehouse, not copied, yet always found. Readers get a warm literary memoir of a Kentucky poet and his circle.
21594-fred-fenton-on-the-crew-or-the-you:
Fred Fenton takes an oar in Allen Chapman's Fred Fenton on the Crew, a volume of the Fred Fenton Athletic Series. Riverport School's young oarsmen train for the big race, shown in the front picture. We win, the caption cries, as Riverport takes the race.

Fred's friend, known far and wide as Bristles for his upright mop of hair, shares the fun. Chapman also wrote the Tom Fairfield and Darewell Chums series for boys. School honour, hard practice, and rivals on the river drive the plot. The tale ends, as the picture promises, with the crew's triumph on the water.
31025-a-new-species-of-pocket-gopher-gen:
Robert J. Russell's 1957 paper names a new pocket gopher, Pappogeomys alcorni, from the high Sierra del Tigre in southern Jalisco, Mexico. Collector J. R. Alcorn had taken gophers across Jalisco, Nayarit, and Colima in 1949 and 1950, and three specimens from that isolated volcanic range proved distinct from their kin.

The type specimen, an adult female taken four miles west of Mazamitla at 6,600 feet in October 1950, anchors the description. It adds notes on its medium size, short naked tail, and skull form. Known only from the higher ground of the Sierra del Tigre, the species shows how a cut-off mountain range can hold a mammal found nowhere else.
31141-four-new-pocket-gophers-of-the-gen:
Robert J. Russell's 1953 paper names four new pocket gophers of the genus Cratogeomys from central Jalisco, Mexico. Two species, gymnurus and zinseri, had been known only from southern and far eastern Jalisco, until collector J. R. Alcorn secured specimens of both in the central part of the state, where study showed two undescribed subspecies of each.

The first described, Cratogeomys gymnurus tellus, rests on an adult female taken three miles west of Tala at 4,300 feet in June 1949, a large, pale, long-tailed gopher. Field costs were met by the National Science Foundation and the Kansas University Endowment Association, and the paper remains the formal record for these central Jalisco forms.
31224-geographic-distribution-of-the-poc:
J. Knox Jones Jr.'s 1953 paper revises the geography of the pocket mouse Perognathus fasciatus, published as volume 5, number 29 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, with seven figures. Osgood's 1900 revision had known two races, and Cary added a pale Wyoming form in 1911, but no important work had followed for forty years.

Thirteen Nebraska specimens from the state's northwest corner matched no known subspecies, prompting Jones to examine material from the whole range. He reduces Perognathus callistus, long treated as a full species, to a subspecies of fasciatus, and names a new subspecies from eastern Wyoming and adjacent Montana, South Dakota, and Nebraska.
34117-beowulf-an-introduction-to-the-stu:
R. W. Chambers's 1921 Cambridge study Beowulf opens the old poem to readers who want more than the tale itself. Part one weighs the history in the poem: the Geats and their kings, Heorot and the Danish kings, and the stories of Offa and Finn.

Later chapters test the Grendel fight against northern parallels, from Grettir to Bothvar Bjarki, and weigh theories of the poem's date, build, and Christian strains. Part two prints source texts, so readers can judge the claims against the records themselves. Chambers dedicates the volume to William Witherle Lawrence, whose printed work and letters aided him.

This collaborative research builds interpretable data-driven models that work across scales, from lab plasmas to space. Understandable AI for one of physics' most violent processes.
doe-osti-3484786-toward-next-generation-: Science runs on software — but the tools are scattered across fields. govdocs-archive_org-noob-flushyourmeds_N:
Scott A. Barry's NOOB #flushyourmeds is an e-book that mixes two subjects few books combine: beginner occult instruction and practical notes on digital privacy. Its title addresses the reader as a noob, a newcomer to both crafts at once.

Alongside occult material and numerology, Barry writes about MAC spoofing and routing traffic through Tor, the tools of staying anonymous online. The text is fragmentary and eclectic, jumping between its worlds without apology. The result is a strange hybrid from the internet's occult underground, where magic and operational security are treated as one art.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AllenMarkFOIASe:
When the House Select Committee on Assassinations took up the murders of John F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr. in the late 1970s, its members and staff needed a common base of background information. This briefing book was prepared for the committee to supply it.

The volume gathers the background the reinvestigation worked from, and it survives here as researcher Mark Allen's FOIA selection, drawn from disclosures dated April 12, 1984. Briefing books show what investigators were told before they began asking questions, which makes them evidence in their own right. The file is a public record of the second official inquiry.
in-bohemia-with-du-maurier-the-first-of-:
Felix Moscheles wrote this memoir of his student days with artist George du Maurier in the fifties. The London book holds sixty-three drawings by du Maurier that show that early life. Moscheles finished the proofs just before news of his friend's death reached him in Venice.

He chose to let the joyous pages stand as du Maurier had approved them. Music binds the friends in the tale, from Leipzig circles to a concert tour in Belgium. Pianist Louis Brassin links them to the master Moscheles. The book preserves a bohemian youth and a deep friendship in art.
nasa-tm-19680005116-parametric-analysis-:
James J. Ward and Robert Ruch, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, analyzed a nuclear power generator in January 1968. The machine turns heat from a radioisotope fuel block into electricity in two cascaded stages. A hot silicon-germanium stage sits inside, wrapped by a cooler lead telluride stage.

Heat leaves through the outer shell, and fins are usually needed to help it escape. Ward and Ruch vary the design parameters to see how performance changes. Such generators power spacecraft far from the Sun, where solar cells fail. The analysis maps the choices a designer must trade against each other.
nasa-tm-19710003531-experimental-determi:
Frank Bugg of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 20, 1970. It measures, by experiment, how fast liquid sloshes in a tilted round tank. The tank is a right circular cylinder set at an incline, like a propellant tank in a climbing rocket.

Bugg tilted the tank at four angles to the vertical and varied the liquid depth as well. Two slosh modes were tracked, told apart by which way the still line across the surface ran. Raising the tilt lowered the slosh frequency of both modes, he reports. The mode tied to the surface's minor axis slowed much more than the other.
nasa-tm-19720022221-s-cubed-a-spacecraft:
S-Cubed A, a Spacecraft and Experiment Description, is a NASA document on the Explorer 45 satellite, called S3-A before launch. The small scientific satellite launched on November 15, 1971, from the San Marco range in Kenya aboard a four-stage Scout rocket. It entered an elliptical equatorial orbit carrying charged particle and field experiments.

The S3 program gave experimenters a small, flexible spacecraft able to fly a well-integrated detector set on the economical Scout. Its data handling system was unusual for its time because it could be reprogrammed from the ground. This description sets out the first mission's scientific objectives, aimed at magnetospheric phenomena in the heart of the magnetosphere. It also defines the orbital parameters, summarizes detector characteristics, and explains the data system's capabilities.
podcast-dannyjones-y3XbBfTqcSc:
Wildlife host Forrest Galante joins Danny Jones to talk about DNA scientists who plan to build a real Jurassic Park by 2027. Galante is a biologist known for hunts for lost species. The plan at issue is de-extinction, the bid to bring back the dead.

Galante walks through the labs that aim to revive lost beasts from old DNA. He weighs which beasts could walk again first and what parks might hold them. Jones asks where the plan could go wrong. Listeners get a wild but real tale from the edge of gene work. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson-DG-dcjlzCsc:
Tucker Carlson declares that the ruling class is losing control. His short title carries the whole thesis of the hour. He points to cracks in media, courts, and party power.

Carlson argues that elite panic shows in bans, suits, and harsh words. Each move, he says, admits that old tools fail. He urges viewers to read fear as a sign of change. The episode is a rallying brief for the hopeful and the rebellious. It gives no guest and no hedge: one host reads the moment as a turning of the tide.
the-dead-men-s-song-being-the-story-of-a: Champion Ingraham Hitchcock wrote The Dead Men's Song as the story of a poem and a sketch of its author, Young Ewing Allison, his friend. The Louisville edition of 1914 was limited to two hundred and fifty copies. Its title promises a browse through other gems of Allison's and recollections of days, with facsimiles of manuscripts folded in. A quote from Walt Mason holds that the man who wrote the poem should not go unknelled, unhonored, and unsung. Only the title pages and front matter are present here.
washington-in-domestic-life-from-origina:
Richard Rush wrote Washington in Domestic Life from original letters and manuscripts in 1857. A letter to his publishers, J. B. Lippincott and Company of Philadelphia, fronts the piece. He tells them plainly that he will answer for any shortfall in the cost of publishing, once their charges for doing the work fitly are paid. If the small piece should by some remote chance yield a profit, he directs that it go, however small, to the Washington Monument Fund.

He calls the work a literary trifle, hardly worth a dedication. Yet he dedicates it to Charles J. Ingersoll all the same. The idea took shape at a dinner at Ingersoll's table, where the new Vice-President, Mr. Breckenridge, sat among the guests. Rush, who had known the world of the early republic, draws on private papers to show Washington at home.
